messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a 40-year-old married software engineer of Syrian descent, living with his wife and two children in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a natural disaster — a tornado that struck his neighbourhood approximately eight months ago, collapsing part of the building where he had been sheltering with colleagues during a work event. The structure partially gave way without warning: a roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once, the crack and groan of beams, the sensation of the floor tilting, debris striking him as he ran. He was trapped for nearly two hours before emergency responders reached him. Several people were seriously injured. Tariq was not hospitalised, but the physical examination he underwent at the scene — the latex-gloved hands, the bright ambulance interior, the clinical smell — left an impression that fused itself to the terror of those two hours. He walked away. He has not felt safe since.

The memories that followed do not arrive as recollections so much as reinstatements. When they come, Tariq hears the sound — the specific grinding collapse of the ceiling — as though it is occurring in the room around him. The sequence refuses to hold still: he cannot say with certainty what happened first, what he did before he ran, whether he called out or was silent, and this disorganisation frightens him almost as much as the content itself. At their worst, the memories return with full sensory force, the smell of dust and insulation, the cold of the floor, the weight of something across his legs — and in those moments he is entirely back there, not remembering but reliving. These intrusions, in turn, have deepened a set of beliefs that have quietly taken over his inner life. He has come to feel that someone else — someone more competent, more alert — would never have been caught in that building, would have read the signs and left earlier. The memory, arriving without warning and without order, seems to confirm to him that he is permanently damaged, that nothing good lies ahead, that the person who once moved through the world with ease and even happiness is simply gone.

Those beliefs, once established, have made the world feel actively dangerous. Tariq is certain, in a way he cannot argue himself out of, that threat is always nearby and that he will be slow to see it. At work — an open-plan office where colleagues move between desks and approach from behind — he finds himself scanning constantly, tracking the periphery of his vision. Unexpected movement nearby sends a jolt of alarm through him before he has time to think. If a colleague places a hand on his shoulder, he flinches hard enough that people have noticed and stopped touching him. Before he can settle anywhere — a meeting room, a restaurant with his wife, even a new section of the office — he locates the exits first. This hypervigilance, exhausting as it is, also keeps the memory close: the body on alert seems to prime the mind for intrusion, and the intrusions, when they come, reinforce his certainty that danger is real and that he cannot trust his own reactions.

To manage all of this, Tariq has developed habits that feel like coping but function as traps. He forces himself, consciously and effortfully, to think only positive thoughts whenever distress rises — a strategy that requires constant mental labour and leaves him feeling fraudulent when the memories break through anyway. He has stopped going anywhere near hospitals or ambulances; a route change he made months ago to avoid the medical centre near his office has quietly become permanent, adding twenty minutes to his commute and raising questions from his wife. The avoidance and the forced positivity together seem to keep the threat system primed — what he will not approach, he cannot learn is safe — and his appraisals of himself as broken and uniquely unfortunate have only hardened. He also finds himself, in quieter moments, running through thoughts about the building's owners and whether they were negligent — a rumination that provides a brief sense of agency but leaves him more agitated than before.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment at his daughter's school recital, when a door slammed backstage and he dropped to a crouch in the aisle. His wife looked at him with an expression he describes as frightened. He sat through the rest of the performance in silence. What he fears most, he said at intake, is that he is right — that he really has become someone who cannot be trusted to hold things together. What he hopes, more quietly, is that he is wrong.
